title: AI cyber scams targeting homebuyers’ deposits
full_text:
Nearly 60 per cent of Australians can’t spot the warning signs of an AI-generated property scam trying to con homebuyers to pay a deposit.
New research from digital settlements platform PEXA has revealed while last year 51 per cent of Australians believed they could identify a fraudulent attempt to cut into their property transaction — the share is now down to 41 per cent.
In NSW, 36 per cent of people surveyed said they could spot a criminal trying to intrude on their home transaction.
When presented with a mock scam email requesting the payment of a deposit, 38 per cent of buyers indicated they would transfer funds after receiving it — against 41 per cent who said the email looked like a scam and would not have paid.
The list of property scam attacks include phishing emails, sale and rental listing scams, dodgy property investment attacks, AI voice cloning, settlement scams and credential stuffing — where a scammer steals the credentials of a trusted person to pretend to be them.
Warning signs included unexpected email addresses, poorly written correspondence and urgent demands for payment.
Out of the list, AI voice cloning was one of the biggest alarm bells — with 61 per cent of Australians aware of it, and 85 per cent of those planning to buy a home in the next year concerned about the impact the digital threat could have on their plans.
PEXA chief information security officer Graham Fairley said with latest Australian Competition and Consumer Commission data showing a 9.3 per cent increase in payment redirection scams from 2024 to 2025, not only were the scammers getting smarter — their volume of attacks was growing too. “It’s definitely rising,” Mr Fairley said. “The size of the sums involved are large … that’s why it is a target and continues to be a target.”
